{{Short description|Family of mathematical functions}}
In [[computability theory]], [[computational complexity theory]] and [[proof theory]], the '''slow-growing hierarchy''' is an [[ordinal number|ordinal]]-indexed family of slowly increasing functions ''g''<sub>''α''</sub>: '''N''' → '''N''' (where '''N''' is the set of [[natural numbers]], {0, 1, ...}). It contrasts with the [[fast-growing hierarchy]].

== Definition ==
Let ''μ'' be a [[large countable ordinal]] such that a [[fundamental sequence (ordinals)|fundamental sequence]] is assigned to every [[limit ordinal]] less than ''μ''.  The '''slow-growing hierarchy''' of functions ''g''<sub>''α''</sub>: '''N''' → '''N''', for ''α'' < ''μ'', is then defined as follows:<ref>J. Gallier, [https://www.cis.upenn.edu/~jean/kruskal.pdf What's so special about Kruskal's theorem and the ordinal Γ<sub>0</sub>? A survey of some results in proof theory] (2012, p.63). Accessed 8 May 2023.</ref>

*<math> g_0(n) = 0 </math>
*<math> g_{\alpha+1}(n) = g_\alpha(n) + 1 </math>
*<math> g_\alpha(n) = g_{\alpha[n]}(n)</math> for limit ordinal ''α''.

Here ''α''[''n''] denotes the ''n''<sup>th</sup> element of the fundamental sequence assigned to the limit ordinal ''α''.

The article on the [[Fast-growing hierarchy#Definition|fast-growing hierarchy]] describes a standardized choice for fundamental sequence for all ''α'' < ε<sub>0</sub>.

==Example==
*<math> g_1(n) = 1 </math>
*<math> g_m(n) = m </math>
*<math> g_\omega(n) = n </math>
*<math> g_{\omega+m}(n) = n+m </math>
*<math> g_{\omega m}(n) = mn </math>
*<math> g_{\omega^m}(n) = n^m </math>
*<math> g_{\omega^\omega}(n) = n^n </math>
*<math> g_{\varepsilon _0}(n) = n\uparrow\uparrow n </math>

== Relation to fast-growing hierarchy ==
The slow-growing hierarchy grows much more slowly than the fast-growing hierarchy. Even ''g''<sub>[[epsilon zero (mathematics)|ε<sub>0</sub>]]</sub> is only equivalent to ''f''<sub>3</sub> and ''g''<sub>''α''</sub> only attains the growth of ''f''<sub>ε<sub>0</sub></sub> (the first function that [[Peano arithmetic]] cannot prove [[total function|total]] in the hierarchy) when ''α'' is the [[Bachmann–Howard ordinal]].<ref name="girard81">{{Cite journal | last1=Girard | first1=Jean-Yves | author1-link=Jean-Yves Girard | title=Π<sup>1</sup><sub>2</sub>-logic. I. Dilators | doi=10.1016/0003-4843(81)90016-4 | mr=656793 | year=1981 | journal=Annals of Mathematical Logic | issn=0003-4843 | volume=21 | issue=2 | pages=75–219 | doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="cichon">{{cite book|last=Cichon|title=Proof Theory|year=1992|publisher=Cambridge University Press|pages=173–193|editor1=P. Aczel |editor2=H. Simmons |editor3=S. Wainer |chapter=Termination Proofs and Complexity Characterisations}}</ref><ref name="wainer83">{{Cite journal | last1=Cichon | first1=E. A. | last2=Wainer | first2=S. S. | title=The slow-growing and the Grzegorczyk hierarchies | doi=10.2307/2273557 | mr=704094 | year=1983 | journal=[[The Journal of Symbolic Logic]] | issn=0022-4812 | volume=48 | issue=2 | pages=399–408 | jstor=2273557 | s2cid=1390729 }}</ref>

However, [[Jean-Yves Girard|Girard]] proved that the slow-growing hierarchy eventually ''catches up'' with the fast-growing one.<ref name="girard81" /> Specifically, that there exists an ordinal ''α'' such that for all integers ''n''
:''g''<sub>''α''</sub>(''n'') < ''f''<sub>''α''</sub>(''n'') < ''g''<sub>''α''</sub>(''n'' + 1)
where ''f''<sub>''α''</sub> are the functions in the fast-growing hierarchy. He further showed that the first ''α'' this holds for is the ordinal of the theory ID<sub><ω</sub> of [[Theories of iterated inductive definitions|arbitrary finite iterations of an inductive definition]].<ref name="wainer89">{{cite journal |jstor=2274873 |pages=608–614 |last1=Wainer |first1=S. S. |title=Slow Growing Versus Fast Growing |volume=54 |issue=2 |journal=The Journal of Symbolic Logic |year=1989 |doi=10.2307/2274873|s2cid=19848720 }}</ref> However, for the assignment of fundamental sequences found in <ref name="cichon" /> the first match up occurs at the level ε<sub>0</sub>.<ref name="weier1997">{{cite journal |doi=10.1016/S0168-0072(97)00033-X |title=Sometimes slow growing is fast growing |year=1997 |last1=Weiermann |first1=A |journal=[[Annals of Pure and Applied Logic]] |volume=90 |issue=1–3 |pages=91–99|doi-access=free }}</ref> For Buchholz style tree ordinals it could be shown that the first match up even occurs at <math>\omega^2</math>.

Extensions of the result proved<ref name="wainer89" /> to considerably larger ordinals show that there are very few ordinals below the ordinal of transfinitely iterated <math>\Pi^1_1</math>-comprehension where the slow- and fast-growing hierarchy match up.<ref name="weier1995">{{cite journal |last=Weiermann |first=A. |year=1995 |title= Investigations on slow versus fast growing: How to majorize slow growing functions nontrivially by fast growing ones|journal= Archive for Mathematical Logic|volume= 34 |issue=5 |pages=313–330 |doi= 10.1007/BF01387511|s2cid=34180265 }}</ref>

The slow-growing hierarchy depends extremely sensitively on the choice of the underlying fundamental sequences.<ref name="weier1997" /><ref name="weier1999">Weiermann, A. (1999), [https://books.google.com/books?id=2IHm3RT2bBoC&pg=PA403 "What makes a (pointwise) subrecursive hierarchy slow growing?"] Cooper, S. Barry (ed.) et al., Sets and proofs. Invited papers from the Logic colloquium '97, European meeting of the Association for Symbolic Logic, Leeds, UK, July 6–13, 1997. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. Lond. Math. Soc. Lect. Note Ser. 258; 403-423.</ref><ref name="weier2001">{{Cite journal |doi = 10.1002/1521-3870(200108)47:3<397::AID-MALQ397>3.0.CO;2-Y|title = Γ<sub>0</sub> May be Minimal Subrecursively Inaccessible|journal = Mathematical Logic Quarterly |volume = 47|issue = 3|pages = 397–408|year = 2001|last1 = Weiermann|first1 = Andreas}}</ref>
